# Lightning session C: Crawling

Day 1, 16:20 · Tobias Schwarz, Jovana Avramovic · lightning · coverage: transcript

Two community talks were recorded: similar URLs (Tobias Schwarz, CTO and Founder, Audisto, from his self-introduction) and why technical SEO still matters in AI search (Jovana Avramovic, SEO Consultant: hand-over 'Joanna' in the speech-to-text, matched to the official speaker list). Transcript from a second attendee recording.

## Claims

- **[Stage]** A community speaker said similar URLs are an indicator of duplicate content, broken links, unnecessary redirects and other technical issues.
  <br><sub>`D1-C397` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Tobias Schwarz) · consistent with Google docs · [What is canonicalization](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/canonicalization), [URL structure best practices for Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/url-structure) · Extended by [D1-C444](D1-S12-q-a.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-11`, the glossary term *Similar URLs*</sub>

- **[Stage]** In a community speaker's definition, similar URLs are technically different URLs that differ in only a small portion of their characters.
  <br><sub>`D1-C398` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Tobias Schwarz) · Used by the glossary term *Similar URLs*</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker showed five kinds of similar URLs on well-known brand sites: a different protocol or host (HTTP vs HTTPS, www vs non-www), different capitalisation, a different number of delimiters such as slashes, a space encoded as %20 in one URL and + in another, and parameters in a different order.
  <br><sub>`D1-C399` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Tobias Schwarz) · consistent with Google docs · [URL structure best practices for Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/url-structure), [What is canonicalization](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/canonicalization) · Used by `DEV-URL-11`, the glossary term *Similar URLs*</sub>

- **[Stage]** To find similar URLs in a URL list, a community speaker first applies basic normalisation that keeps the meaning: lowercase the scheme and host, remove default ports such as 80 for HTTP, resolve relative path segments and usually drop the fragment, which matters only to clients.
  <br><sub>`D1-C400` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Tobias Schwarz) · consistent with Google docs · [URL structure best practices for Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/url-structure) · Used by `DEV-URL-11`</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker then derives a uniform URL that deliberately changes the meaning (one scheme, everything lowercase, www and index files such as index.html removed, duplicate and trailing delimiters removed, parameters sorted alphabetically) and sorts the URL list by it, so that similar URLs group together.
  <br><sub>`D1-C401` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Tobias Schwarz)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Similar URLs usually come from programming errors or manually set links, but anyone can link to them from other sites, including malicious actors, so a site should be hardened against them.
  <br><sub>`D1-C402` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Tobias Schwarz) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-URL-11`</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker advised that a web application compute the expected URL for every request, for example with reverse routing from the page type and ID, and redirect or return an error page when the requested URL differs.
  <br><sub>`D1-C403` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Tobias Schwarz) · consistent with Google docs · [How to specify a canonical URL with rel="canonical" and other methods](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls) · Repeated by [D1-C445](D1-S12-q-a.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-11`</sub>

- **[Stage]** For query parameters, a community speaker advised checking that every parameter in a request is actually used and in the expected order, and otherwise redirecting to the expected URL with only the used parameters in the correct order.
  <br><sub>`D1-C404` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Tobias Schwarz) · consistent with Google docs · [Managing crawling of faceted navigation URLs](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/faceted-navigation) · Extends [D1-C102](D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-11`</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker said most web applications wrongly accept a numeric ID in a URL written with leading zeros or as a decimal with trailing zeros, which creates further similar URLs, so such variants are worth testing.
  <br><sub>`D1-C405` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Tobias Schwarz)</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker said that more than half of internet traffic in the previous year (2025) was non-human; the source of the figure was not named.
  <br><sub>`D1-C406` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Jovana Avramovic) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker cited more than 900 million weekly active ChatGPT users and 2.5 billion monthly users of a Google AI feature (the recording is unclear which), adding that these are not comparable market-share figures.
  <br><sub>`D1-C407` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Jovana Avramovic) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker argued that search no longer happens in one place, so SEO is about how content is found, understood and trusted wherever search occurs.
  <br><sub>`D1-C408` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Jovana Avramovic)</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker argued that the change in search behaviour is not only longer AI Mode queries but conversation: a follow-up such as 'compare these two' relies on the context of earlier turns.
  <br><sub>`D1-C409` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Jovana Avramovic)</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker described a cognitive offloading shift: people increasingly hand remembering, comparing, analysing and even decision-making over to search tools.
  <br><sub>`D1-C410` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Jovana Avramovic)</sub>

- **[Stage]** In a community speaker's view, AI search changes the workflow but not the foundation: where one query once returned ten blue links and left research and comparison to the user, one query can now lead to many different answers.
  <br><sub>`D1-C411` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Jovana Avramovic)</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker described AI search as turning one query into many related searches, including searches in other languages, before the information is retrieved.
  <br><sub>`D1-C412` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Jovana Avramovic) · consistent with Google docs · [AI features and your website](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features) · Extends [D1-C053](D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker said technical SEO remains the foundation for AI search, with site architecture showing the structure and thematic connections of content and structured data adding clarity, but that a technically sound site is only the beginning.
  <br><sub>`D1-C413` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Jovana Avramovic)</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker linked the serial-position effect in human memory (people best remember the first and last items of a list) to the 'lost in the middle' pattern that research has found in large language models.
  <br><sub>`D1-C414` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Jovana Avramovic) · not in Google docs · Used by the glossary term *Lost in the middle*</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker advised placing the most important information at the beginning or the end of a piece of content, because information in the middle is less likely to be cited by AI systems.
  > "It's relevant to put your most important information at the beginning or at the end."
  <br><sub>`D1-C415` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Jovana Avramovic)</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker reported that on client sites information towards the end of the content got cited, and invited others to check their own examples.
  <br><sub>`D1-C416` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Jovana Avramovic)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Placing key facts first or last is a community heuristic based on research into language models, not something Google has said its systems do; Google's own advice (D1-C054) is to write for people without chopping content, and a short summary at the top serves readers either way.
  <br><sub>`D1-C417` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling · Used by the glossary term *Lost in the middle*</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker summed up the shift as SEO's target expanding rather than moving: besides asking whether a page can rank, ask whether its information is useful as a source and easy to extract.
  > "The target is not shifting; it is expanding."
  <br><sub>`D1-C418` · Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling (Jovana Avramovic)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Of the two answers a community speaker offered for a request to a URL variant (redirect, or an error page), Google's canonicalization guide favours the redirect: a redirect is a strong signal that its target should become canonical, while an error page throws away any links pointing at the variant.
  <br><sub>`D1-C421` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling · [How to specify a canonical URL with rel="canonical" and other methods](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls)</sub>
